cards.note: The earliest written Chinese account is a book first published in 1549, not 1550, and the sources give no Yangtze location; Boylston places it in China generally. The 1567 to 1572 first-practice date is Needham's, reported second-hand, so it is not used. Priority against Indian inoculation is unresolved.
cards.name: Smallpox inoculation by nasal insufflation in China
cards.summary: Chinese practitioners blew powdered smallpox scabs up the nose to give deliberate protection, recorded in writing from 1549.
cards.description: By 1549 a Chinese book describes variolation, the deliberate transfer of smallpox material into a healthy person, usually by blowing powdered scabs up the nostril. Boylston, reviewing Needham, reports that this was the earliest written discussion in China and that the practice was probably older than the text.
cards.origin_note: The earliest written account known is Chinese, but Boylston notes that an Indian origin has also been proposed, so priority is not settled.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: deliberate protection against a disease, and by 1700 a description of the Chinese insufflation method had reached England.

events.statement: The earliest written discussion of variolation in China is in a book first published in 1549.
events.quote: The earliest written discussion of variolation in China is found in a book first published in 1549.

sources.title: The origins of inoculation
sources.publisher: Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine

open_questions: Which 1549 book is meant? Wan Quan's text is named in secondary sources but I did not open it.
Whether Ottoman and Indian inoculation descend from the Chinese practice or arose separately.

cards.note: Nature dates the chance discovery of attenuation to 1879, not 1880. Its anthrax vaccine was attenuated by potassium dichromate, a process similar to Toussaint's, according to Chamberland's notebooks, so the lead's claim that Pasteur's method was original needs care. The sources give no Pouilly-le-Fort site coordinates, so the place is recorded at country level.
cards.name: Laboratory-attenuated vaccines by Pasteur in France
cards.summary: Pasteur weakened microbes in the laboratory to make vaccines, from chicken cholera in 1879 to rabies in 1885.
cards.description: In 1879 Pasteur found by chance that cultures of the chicken cholera bacterium gradually lost virulence, and that the weakened cultures protected birds. In May 1881 a public trial at Pouilly-le-Fort vaccinated sheep, a goat and cows with an anthrax vaccine, and in July 1885 Pasteur first treated a person bitten by a rabid dog with his rabies vaccine.
cards.origin_note: Nature describes attenuation as Pasteur's own discovery in his laboratory, and it was prompted by Jenner's vaccination, which is not an earlier achievement of the same thing.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: a general method for making vaccines from weakened microbes, which Nature presents as the basis for later vaccine work.

events.statement: In 1879 Pasteur found by chance that cultures of the chicken cholera bacterium gradually lost their virulence.
events.quote: In 1879, Pasteur discovered by chance that cultures of this bacterium gradually lost their virulence over time.

cards.name: Clonal selection theory of immunity by Burnet in Melbourne
cards.summary: Frank Macfarlane Burnet's 1957 theory that each immune cell makes one antibody and infection selects the cells that fit, tested in 1958.
cards.description: In 1957 Frank Macfarlane Burnet published the clonal selection theory of immunity, in which each immune cell recognises one foreign material and multiplies when it meets its match. In 1958 Gus Nossal and Joshua Lederberg, working at the Walter and Eliza Hall Institute in Melbourne, showed that a single immune cell makes only one type of antibody, the first experimental proof of the theory.
cards.origin_note: WEHI presents the theory as Burnet's own work, built on Jerne's natural selection theory, and no earlier clonal selection account appears in the sources I opened.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: it explained immune memory and the match between cells and antigens, and WEHI calls the 1958 result the first experimental proof of the theory.

cards.why: WEHI says Burnet was struggling with self-marker ideas, and that Jerne's natural selection theory made sense of antibody formation once cells were seen as selected by contact with an antigen.

events.statement: In 1957 Frank Macfarlane Burnet published a new theory of the immune system, the clonal selection theory.

cards.name: Experimental psychology laboratory of Wundt at Leipzig
cards.summary: Wilhelm Wundt's laboratory at Leipzig, recognised by the university in 1879, is treated as the first laboratory devoted to psychology.
cards.description: In 1879 the University of Leipzig formally recognised Wilhelm Wundt's room of equipment as a laboratory, which the Stanford Encyclopedia calls the world's first devoted to psychology. Students built much of the apparatus and performed the experiments there, under Wundt's direction of research.
cards.origin_note: The Stanford Encyclopedia describes the Leipzig room as the world's first laboratory devoted to psychology, so it is the earliest known in these sources.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the laboratory was the first devoted to psychology, and it trained the students who built and ran its experiments.

cards.why: The Stanford Encyclopedia says the soil was prepared by Fechner, Weber and Lotze, and that Leipzig's philosophy department provided the setting for Wundt's work.

cards.note: The treatment that gave the talking cure ran from 1880 to 1882, so the practice dates from 1880 rather than 1895; 1895 is the publication of Studies on Hysteria. Britannica credits Pappenheim with suggesting the approach, and Breuer's account of a full recovery is disputed. The lead's comparison with hypnotic suggestion, moral treatment and later trial-tested therapies is not covered by the sources I opened.
cards.name: Talking cure of Breuer and Pappenheim in Vienna
cards.summary: Josef Breuer's treatment of Bertha Pappenheim from 1880 to 1882 used talking and made-up stories as a cure, published in 1895.
cards.description: From 1880 to 1882 Josef Breuer treated Bertha Pappenheim, known as Anna O., in a treatment approach she suggested, in which she expressed her thoughts through made-up stories, which they called the talking cure. Breuer's case was published in Studies on Hysteria in 1895, jointly with Sigmund Freud, which Victorian Web calls the early psychoanalytical publication.
cards.origin_note: The sources show the talking cure was developed in this treatment, but I did not check whether earlier talking or hypnotic treatments were its precursors, so priority is not settled.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the case began the psychoanalytic line of treatment by conversation, which Victorian Web credits to Breuer's proto-psychoanalytic technique.

cards.why: Victorian Web says Anna O. had proven resistant to suggestion in the hypnoid state, and her many distressing symptoms persisted.

cards.lead: Lithium treatment of mania in Australia
cards.note: Schioldann dates Cade's clinical trial from 29 March 1948 to 11 February 1949, so the work began in 1948 and was published in 1949. The first controlled trial was Schou's Risskov study, reported in 1954, which the lead names only as Schou's trials. The sources give Melbourne as the place of the case records, not a precise trial site.
cards.name: Lithium treatment of mania by Cade in Melbourne
cards.summary: John Cade's 1948 to 1949 trial of lithium salts calmed manic patients, the first modern drug treatment for a mental disorder.
cards.description: Between 29 March 1948 and 11 February 1949 John Cade recorded his observations on ten manic patients, and his 1949 paper reported on them. A controlled Danish trial at Risskov, reported in 1954, confirmed lithium's antimanic effect.
cards.origin_note: Schioldann treats Cade's 1949 work as the start of lithium therapy for mania in these sources; I did not check earlier non-psychiatric uses of lithium.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: lithium was the first modern drug for a mental disorder, though its adoption came about two decades later.
